notes: A partnership was not a legal entity and so could not own property (18); the courts throughout the period refused to treat deed-of-settlement companies as anything other than partnerships (43-46); 'Partnerships do not have legal personality' (150). ENTITY LOCATOR, 2026-08-31 RULE: the entity is the company as the deed of settlement scopes it - the joint stock the shareholder-partners are members of - and NOT the body of trustees. Televantos writes that the trustees 'acted as the legal personality for the firm' (38); that is a functional substitute supplied by a device inside the arrangement, not personhood in the arrangement, and reading the trustees as the entity would make LP1-LP3 answer a question about three named individuals rather than about the company. The trust fund is NOT a sub-pool for locator purposes - it is the whole arrangement's circulating assets - so the sub-pool exclusion does not bite on this row.

The company could not own property. Legal title to the circulating trade assets was settled on a fixed body of trustees, and the shareholder-partners were equitable co-owners of the joint stock, no partner being able to claim any particular asset of the firm as his own (18, 37-38). The capacity that fails is capacity in the COMPANY, which had none; the trustee device is how the arrangement worked around that, and it is recorded here rather than coded. Entity locator as at LP1.

STRUCTURAL HALF, NOT A HEDGE, AND THE CELL A REVIEWER SHOULD LOOK AT FIRST. At common law the deed of settlement provided that the firm's litigation be conducted in the trustees' names alone, and this worked: the trustees held legal title to company property and to the debts owed the business and could sue on them in their own names 'without reference to the fluctuating body of shareholder-partners' (38; Metcalf v Bruin (1810), Lord Ellenborough CJKB). In Chancery it failed: joinder required every shareholder-partner as a party, Lord Eldon would not routinely dispense with it, and these companies 'could not reliably sue or be sued in Chancery' (50). Televantos's own summary is that 'a company could not sue in its own name, rather than that of its shareholders or trustees, without an Act of Parliament' (172). Read as the trustees the cell is 1; read as the company 0; read as the whole arrangement, which is what the 2026-08-31 locator rule requires, it is P. ALTERNATIVE READING STATED FAIRLY: a coder who held that standing exercised only through named natural persons is not standing in the entity would code 0, and the evidence for that is preserved here.

The jingle rule. On the partners' bankruptcy the joint estate was administered as a distinct estate and distributed to partnership creditors in priority to each partner's separate creditors (22-23, 145; Ex p Ruffin (1801)). TELEVANTOS'S OWN EVIDENCE, NOT A RESTATEMENT OF HKS: the cell rests on Lord Eldon's judgments, the Bankruptcy Court order books (record class B 1) and Eldon's judicial notebooks. HKS is the frame he argues with, and at 144 he says in terms that Hansmann, Kraakman and Squire 'overlook limitations on partnership law's ability to preserve business assets for business creditors'. ARTICULATED on Lord Eldon's own words in Ex p Ruffin, quoted at 165: the joint creditors 'had clearly no lien whatsoever upon the partnership effects ... the equity is not that of the joint creditors, but that of the partners with regard to each other, that operates to the payment of the partnership debts'. THE PRIORITY IS DERIVATIVE AND DEFEASIBLE: it ran by subrogation to the partners' rights of indemnity and lien, so where the partners voluntarily discharged the lien by transferring the assets to a continuing partner the priority vanished - Ruffin's actual holding (166) - and 'Partnership creditors could thus never be safe from partners, by private agreement, emptying the partnership estate and so rendering their claims worthless' (168). That defeasibility is recorded here and NOT coded, because whether members can strip the pool is AP2's question.

STRUCTURAL HALF. Members' creditors: a separate creditor levying judgment against a partner's share could claim only that partner's right to the residue after the partnership creditors had been paid (148) - shielding present, and by a substantive rule. Members: as a matter of substantive law any partner could dissolve at will (24), which would partition the pool; in practice shareholders 'could not easily use the courts to dissolve or withdraw their capital from such concerns', and 'the difficulty shareholders had in suing such entities de facto acted as a capital lock-in mechanism' (51-52). Televantos states expressly that this was 'a by-product of what was, in effect, a rejection of jurisdiction over such companies, rather than a substantive rule of law' (51), and he rejects Morley's reading of Van Sandau v Moore (1826) as designed to lock capital in (50). WELL-FORMEDNESS FLAG, RAISED AND NOT REPAIRED: AP2 asks two questions - can members force partition, and can their creditors - and this pair of rows separates them. See the compagnie_antwerpen AP2 note: both rows read P and the two P's are not the same state, so this is not agreement.

Shareholders of a deed-of-settlement company were in law partners of the firm and so 'personally liable without limit for the firm's debts' (44); clauses in the deed purporting to give them limited liability 'were not fully effective', creditors being able to sue shareholders personally unless they had agreed not to (45); and 'the directors and shareholders of such companies were treated as personally liable for the debts of the firm' (172). ARTICULATED on Lord Ellenborough's words in R v Dodd (1808), quoted at 46: 'As to the subscribers themselves, indeed, they may stipulate with each other for this contracted responsibility; but as to the rest of the world it is clear that each partner is liable to the whole amount of the debts contracted by the partnership.' LOCATOR: CF1=P puts the locator on the labour-party, here the directors, and 172 answers for them directly; the cell is unchanged on the members fallback, since shareholder-partners and directors alike were liable without limit. DISAGREEMENT RECORDED, NOT RESOLVED: John Morley argues the trust did give shareholders limited liability; Televantos answers that the argument 'would have surprised contemporaries' (45-46). ONE DATUM, TWO CELLS: the R v Dodd passage carries this cell and LR1.

No founder. The company was constituted by subscription under a deed of settlement, not by an endowment out of an identifiable founder's patrimony, so the 2026-08-30 AP4 rule returns .NA and not 0. That is a form on which AP4 might take a value other than 1. See the notes file. Default partnership law dissolved the firm on any partner's death, retirement, bankruptcy, or simply at will, and even a new partner joining dissolved the old partnership and joint estate and created a new one (24, 150). Settling the assets on a fixed body of trustees was 'designed to insulate the company from the effect of the rules effecting mandatory partnership dissolution upon any change of partners, which could have been particularly troublesome in concerns with hundreds or even thousands of shareholder-partners' (38). It did not make the company persist as a legal unit - the courts treated these firms as partnerships throughout (43-46), and Chapter 7's Rule IV is that a single business in fact could in law be a succession of separate partnership estates (150) - but it did carry the asset-holding across the change of members. Half-present: the pool survives the member's exit, the entity does not. NOT CODED 1: Televantos nowhere says the device achieved succession. The substantive right survived and the remedy did not. Any partner could dissolve the firm unilaterally at any time (24), and since the courts treated deed-of-settlement companies as partnerships the rule reached them; but Lord Eldon's Chancery would not entertain the suit, so shareholders 'could not easily use the courts to dissolve or withdraw their capital from such concerns' (51). One common fund - the joint stock - vested in a fixed body of trustees who held the circulating partnership assets (37); the partners were equitable co-owners and 'no partner could claim any particular asset of the firm as his own' (18). The partners' 'separate estates' are their own patrimonies, not sub-pools of the entity, so nothing here engages the sub-pool exclusion. Per logbook 1, 2026-08-31 (ii): CI1 records how many pools there are and cannot record that this one was held through a trust, which is the fact that distinguishes the form.

A partner's interest in the joint stock was residual. Each partner's right of indemnity was secured by an equitable lien over the others' shares, so no partner could claim any asset of the firm personally until the firm's creditors had been paid and an account taken (19-20), and a partner could not withdraw his stock from a factually insolvent firm because his share was then 'a liability rather than an asset' (147; West v Skipp (1749), quoted). For this form the effect was reinforced procedurally, shareholders being unable to use the courts to withdraw capital (51-52). CAUTION ON THE FRAME: Televantos cites Blair's 'locking in capital' only as part of the hindsight narrative he is criticising (28 n 91), and on his own account the lock-in here is a by-product of a jurisdictional refusal rather than a doctrine (51). One datum with AP2's second limb and TS3.

Deed-of-settlement companies excluded the default partnership rule by providing expressly that partners could alienate their shares (36), and the trust made transfer effective by entry in the company's own books, operating as an assignment of the equitable interest by a direction to hold to the use of another (37; Ashby v Blackwell (1765)). TWO QUALIFICATIONS CARRIED, NOT RESOLVED: directors were typically given a veto over transfers (36 n 45); and free transferability was the very feature that exposed the company to prosecution under the Bubble Act until its repeal in 1825, and thereafter to Lord Eldon's view that raising sums by selling freely alienable shares without Act or Charter remained an offence at common law (40, 43, 172). Confidence medium for that reason: the clauses were drafted and used, their lawfulness was never settled.

Half-present. In form the interest was negotiable: shares changed hands by book entry (37) and were dealt in by stockbrokers - Josephs v Pebrer (1825) is a broker suing a client for unpaid shares (39) - amid a promotion boom that floated 624 companies in 1824-25 (39). In substance the holder's identity kept mattering: directors held a veto over transfers, every holder remained personally liable without limit, and Lord Eldon proposed a shareholder register precisely so that creditors could identify and sue them, with transfers null until registration (45). Televantos, following Ireland, dates the impersonal market in shares and the consequent separation of company from partnership to later in the century (44). CI4=P with CI3=1 is consistent with the declared entailment.

Each partner was 'liable to the whole amount of the debts contracted by the partnership' (R v Dodd (1808), Lord Ellenborough CJKB, quoted at 46). The form is JOINT rather than joint-and-several on Televantos's own framing: Chapter 7's Rule IV is titled and argued as 'Joint Creditors Have Rights against the Partners' Jointly, not a Firm' (149-151), and a creditor remained a creditor of the partners as they stood when the debt was contracted, unless he had accepted the new partners in lieu. LOCATOR: as at AP3, robust to CF1=P (directors, answered at 172) and to the members fallback. ONE DATUM, TWO CELLS with AP3, and see LR6.

The decision-makers - directors, themselves shareholder-partners - were personally liable without limit for the firm's debts (172), so they were bound to the venture's outcomes. RECORDED AS DISAGREEMENT, NOT RESOLVED: the contemporary charge against joint-stock trading, which Televantos reports at length and does not endorse, is precisely that the split of ownership from management attenuated that exposure - Adam Smith on directors as 'the managers rather of other people's money than their own' (30), Godwin on directors 'fattened on the vitals of their fellow citizens' (30), and Gisborne's proposal that directors hold a large shareholding 'to make them more like partners' (30). A coder persuaded by the contemporaries would code 'attenuated'; the legal fact codes 'coupled'. Confidence medium for that reason. ARTICULATED on William Watson, A Treatise of the Law of Partnership (2nd edn 1807) 1, quoted at 17: a partnership is 'a voluntary contract, between two or more persons, for joining together their money, goods, labour, and skill, or either or all of them, upon an agreement that the gain or loss shall be divided proportionally between them'. Partners were presumed equally entitled to the joint stock and profits absent contrary agreement (18), and shareholders were partners 'by definition in having pooled assets for the purpose of running business of which they were to receive a profit' (44). QUALIFICATION CARRIED, NOT RESOLVED: Televantos says Watson's definition 'was not quite accurate' and quotes Lord Eldon in Ex p Langdale (1811) that a man 'may also be a partner, when the contract is that he shall suffer no loss ... the true criterion is, whether they are to participate in profit' (17). Confidence medium for that reason. Constituted by a private deed of settlement with no Royal Charter, patent or Act of Parliament, and that absence is the form's defining feature rather than an incident of it. It is also what made it precarious: the Bubble Act 1720 made it a criminal offence to purport to act as a corporation or to raise capital by issuing transferable stock without such authority (35), and after the Act's repeal in 1825 Lord Eldon held that doing so remained an offence at common law (43), saying in Van Sandau v Moore (1826) that the very 'inconvenience or impracticability of dealing with them in a court of justice, proved bodies of that kind to be illegal at common law' (50). ARTICULATION analyst-imposed: the four-value taxonomy is the analyst's comparative concept, even though the tradition's own words are on the page.

Trading concerns: London corn factors, fire insurance companies, metal companies in Birmingham and the Midlands including Matthew Boulton's, and the Birmingham Flour and Bread Company (36), and the country banks whose collapses in 1810-11 and 1825-26 generate much of the litigation (150). Televantos's glossary defines the form as 'a business which raised capital by issuing shares and/or bonds' (183).

An observed absence, not a silence: the question is squarely put throughout. Corporate status and the privileges attached to it lay in the gift of Crown or Parliament and were granted to quasi-public entities such as canal companies and overseas trading companies (3); the deed-of-settlement company held no charter, patent or franchise; and Lord Eldon's objection to it was that raising large sums by selling freely transferable shares 'involved usurping privileges properly belonging to the Crown and Parliament' (40) - that is, holding none. Contrast compagnie_antwerpen FP2=.NR, where the source never puts the question and a 0 would launder a silence.

DEFINITION UNDERDETERMINED, FLAGGED AND NOT REPAIRED. FP3 reads 'the form confers legal-status or access arbitrage for its principals', and the census's worked instance is identity-masking (the nacion flamenca). Televantos supplies abundant evidence of a different thing - a form used to obtain corporate-like advantages without the Crown's grant - and his finding is that it largely failed to do so, the courts treating these companies as ordinary partnerships and eliciting no more than 'bare tolerance of their existence' (43-46, 52, 172). Which of the two questions FP3 asks decides whether this row is P or .NR. Left .NR pending the maintainer's fix; the evidence is here either way.

Unregistered, and on the courts' own account illegible. There was no register of shareholders; Lord Eldon PROPOSED one in June 1824 precisely so that creditors of such companies 'could identify and sue the shareholders more easily' and never brought his bill in (45, 51); and registration arrived only with the Joint Stock Companies Act 1844, which forced large partnerships to incorporate by registration, 'bringing them within the law and the jurisdiction of the courts' (52). The row's period claim ends at 1844 for exactly this reason: the Act is where this cell would flip.

Half-present, and flagged for comparative-concept hygiene (Haspelmath; CHARACTER-CODING test 3). Televantos's own glossary makes the split constitutive: a deed-of-settlement company 'was distinct from a typical partnership, where the partners who managed the business provided the capital' (183), its deeds provided 'for a split in the firm's ownership and management' (44), and shareholder-partners had no individual powers of management (37) - against the typical partnership, in which 'partners were both owners and managers of the business' (29). But the managers were themselves shareholder-partners, not a party supplying labour instead of capital, so this is an owner/manager separation and not the capital-labour contract CF1 was built around (the commenda family). Coded P and not 1 for that reason. CONSEQUENCE: CF1=P puts AP3's and LR1's locator on the labour-party; both cells are unchanged on either reading, and their notes say so.

'Durante los siglos xvi y xvii en Amberes y Amsterdam, no se desarrollo ningun concepto de velo corporativo' (239) - a statement about both phases. De ruysscher's footnote 2 adds that calling a company a universitas 'no era tipica de la tradicion del ius commune y es posterior a la aparicion de las normas que separan los activos personales de los relacionados con la empresa' (237 n 2). The earliest text distinguishing the manager's own person from the company's is Salgado de Somoza's Labyrinthus creditorum of 1653 (262), which post-dates both phases and belongs to the Amsterdam section. The partners remained the owners: in the ius commune tradition 'se consideraba importante que los socii siguieran siendo propietarios de sus inversiones durante el tiempo que durase la sociedad' (253), and even a passive participante was 'copropietario del capital de la empresa' (258). Assets could be EARMARKED to company debts without the company owning them - the assignments 'No equivalian a un ius in rem para los acreedores sobre los activos de la empresa, sino mas bien a una primera concepcion de que los activos podian ser de una empresa' (248) - and 'en Amberes, la asignacion de bienes a empresas siguio siendo limitada' (264), which De ruysscher writes of the whole period. Coded 0 on capacity, with the earmarking carried here. Partnership claims were not even docketed as such: 'A menudo, se identificaba una sociedad con el socio-administrador o el agente asalariado (factor) y, como resultado, la sociedad en si no importaba si el administrador disponia de suficientes fondos', and unpaid creditors 'reclamaban lo debido a la persona con quien habian firmado el contrato, esto es, el administrador de la empresa' (242). The coding follows his reading and preserves the datum against it. One common fund. Roman law, followed in Antwerp practice, required that company debts be paid out of the communis, 'es decir, los activos conjuntamente adquiridos y los fondos de la societas' (245); Baldus referred the company fund to a corpus and by the late fourteenth century the partners were said to commit 'el capitale de la societas' (250-251). Stracca held each society's capitale distinct even where the partners were the same (251), which makes parallel companies separate arrangements rather than sub-pools of one. SUB-POOL RECORDED, NOT CODED: from the mid sixteenth century Antwerp contracts began to carry a 'fuori del corpo' clause under which preferential withdrawals were paid 'desde un fondo separado, dentro del fondo general de la compania', composed of additional investments or accumulated profits (247). That is internal partitioning; per the 2026-08-31 rule it has no column, is carried here and NOT in confidence. De ruysscher adds that such clauses 'seguian siendo poco frecuentes' (247). STRUCTURAL HALF, AND IT IS DE RUYSSCHER'S OWN THESIS THAT PRODUCES IT. Against lock-in: partners routinely withdrew substantial sums from the company's funds before liquidation, the legal character of those withdrawals - dividend, advance, or loan - 'era a menudo una cuestion delicada', most partnership contracts said nothing about them, and 'El problema juridico era por ende real y la solucion poco clara' (246-247). For lock-in: the canon-law strand held that in a mixed societas ad lucrum the communio covered the investments as well as the profits, so 'los importes invertidos quedaban bloqueados, puesto que una retirada de estos importes suponia el final de la sociedad' - a rule devised to protect active partners who contributed no money (254). De ruysscher's finding is that the Antwerp legislators 'no eligieron entre estas tres opciones, sino que adoptaron las tres' (254), so both rules were in force at once. THAT COEXISTENCE IS THE HALF-PRESENCE, and it is a structural state, not a hedge; uncertainty about which rule governed a given case is carried in confidence, separately. One datum with TS3. SEPARATES FROM compagnie_antwerpen_1582, AND THE HALF IS THE POINT. The rule exists: 'la recopilacion de 1608 estipulaba por primera vez que los contratos de sociedad debian registrarse ante notario, y que cualquier reclamacion derivada de un contrato de sociedad escrito en privado se consideraba nula y sin efecto' (255). So from 1608 the society is in principle registered and legible to the municipal authority, which it was not before. The diffusion failed: the compendium 'no tuvo mucha influencia y el de 1582 siguio siendo el mas importante en la ciudad', its burdensome commercial formalities 'no se acogieron favorablemente', it was never printed, and its 3,643 articles made manuscript copying so laborious that circulation was obstructed (255). AGAINST THAT, AND WHY THIS IS P AND NOT 0: the Antwerp government did order the city court to apply the 1608 chapters on mercantile agreements (255), so the rule was not a dead letter but a poorly diffused one. A rule in force and badly circulated is half-present. Confidence medium, and a coder who weighted the failure of diffusion over the order to apply would code 0.

Half-present, and flagged for comparative-concept hygiene.
